summary.headline: The Select Board reviewed the FY25 audit showing strong reserves, revoted to support $25M in road borrowing, and approved May election ballot questions.
summary.summary: At its April 7 meeting, the Select Board received Southborough's FY25 independent audit, which issued a clean opinion and reported $7.1 million in reserves while highlighting rising OPEB and county pension liabilities. The board adopted five municipal financial policies and assigned members to revise policies regarding grant oversight and the senior tax work-off program. Members also revoted 4-0-1 to recommend Town Meeting Article 13 for $25 million in road borrowing, and unanimously placed debt exclusion questions on the May 12 election ballot.

topics.title: FY25 independent financial audit presentation
topics.summary: Tony Roselli of Roselli, Clark & Associates presented the town's FY25 audit, issuing an unmodified clean opinion for the fifth consecutive year. Southborough's reserve balances rose from 9.4 percent to 11.7 percent of general fund expenditures, helping preserve the town's AAA bond rating. Roselli cautioned that long-term liabilities pose significant future pressure, specifically an $11.4 million surge in the other postemployment benefits (OPEB) liability and an underfunded Worcester County pension system.
key_details: Reserves reached $7.1 million (11.7 percent of expenditures), exceeding the state average of 10 percent and supporting Southborough's AAA rating.
FY25 local receipts beat revenue projections by $2.2 million and departmental spending came in $1.8 million under budget, balanced against $3.3 million in planned free cash use.
Total OPEB liability jumped by $11.4 million to $54.4 million due to medical premium inflation, census adjustments, and retiree longevity, while the OPEB trust fund holds $4.6 million.
The Worcester County pension system is only 52.7 percent funded, likely triggering annual assessment increases of 10 percent to 11.7 percent or more to meet state full-funding mandates.
Roselli recommended the town consider establishing a dedicated pension stabilization fund to cushion anticipated assessment increases.
topics.outcome: Audit presentation accepted; board requested town staff coordinate with the Worcester County actuary for a follow-up discussion on April 28.
topics.why_it_matters: The audit affirms the town's top credit rating and fiscal reserves, but warns of mounting pension and retiree healthcare liabilities that will increase future budget assessments.

topics.title: Routine business
topics.summary: The board handled administrative announcements, upcoming meeting scheduling, and the consent agenda. Members agreed to adjust the start time of the May 19 meeting to accommodate remote participation for a traveling member.
key_details: Announced the annual town employee breakfast scheduled for Monday at 7:30 AM, with approximately 60 RSVPs.
Agreed to move the start time of the May 19 Select Board meeting up to 6:00 PM to accommodate a member traveling in Europe.
Approved the single-item consent agenda by unanimous vote.
Adjourned at the conclusion of the agenda.
topics.outcome: Consent agenda approved 5-0; May 19 meeting rescheduled to 6:00 PM; meeting adjourned.

topics.title: Downtown wayfinding signage survey update
topics.summary: Staff reported on a state One Stop grant funding a downtown wayfinding signage study conducted with consultant Stantec. A public survey is open online, and paper copies are being distributed at key town locations. Staff requested an extension on the survey deadline from the consultant to gather more public input.
key_details: The current grant funds the study, design, and branding process, but does not cover sign fabrication or installation.
Paper copies of the survey are being delivered to the Senior Center, Colonial Gardens, and the Southborough Library.
Staff requested an extension on the public survey beyond the initial end-of-week cutoff.
Survey results will be compiled and made available to the public and the board once completed.

topics.title: Municipal financial policies review and adoption
topics.summary: The board reviewed proposed financial policies formulated in response to state Division of Local Services recommendations. Members voted to formally adopt five uncontested policies while holding three policies for additional editing and committee feedback.
key_details: Voted 5-0 to approve policies for investments, ambulance receivables, anti-fraud controls, reconciliations, and revenue turnover.
Held the Annual Budget Process policy to await input from the Advisory Committee regarding committee sponsorship of the budget article and wording on free cash reliance.
Discussed the Grants Management policy, focusing on adding safeguards before applying for grants that carry recurring personnel or equipment replacement obligations.
Discussed amending the Senior Tax Work-Off policy to align household income limits with other town assistance programs ($60,000) and expanding available slots from 30 to 40 or 50.
Marguerite Landry agreed to lead redrafting for the grants policy, and Al Hamilton agreed to redraft the senior tax work-off policy.
topics.outcome: Five policies approved 5-0; budget, grant, and senior tax work-off policies held for further revision and scheduled to return April 28.

topics.title: Annual Town Meeting Article 13 recommendation revote
topics.summary: The board revisited its position on Annual Town Meeting Article 13, which authorizes borrowing up to $25 million across multiple years for comprehensive town road maintenance. The board had previously split 3-2 in support of the article, but revoted after clarifying member positions regarding operational versus capital budget lines.
key_details: Article 13 authorizes borrowing up to $25 million to fund town-wide roadway and pavement management.
A board member who previously opposed the recommendation changed her vote to support the article, citing the critical necessity of road repairs.
Board member Al Hamilton voted to abstain, stating he supports presenting the $25 million borrowing to Town Meeting for debate but does not endorse the article language as written.
The board discussed making the 2026 pavement management implementation plan handout publicly available ahead of Town Meeting.
topics.outcome: Select Board voted 4-0-1 to recommend approval of Article 13 at Annual Town Meeting.
topics.why_it_matters: The board endorsed a $25 million multi-year borrowing plan to repair and resurface Southborough roads, which must pass both Town Meeting and the ballot box.

topics.title: May 12 annual election debt exclusion ballot questions
topics.summary: The board voted to place debt exclusion questions on the ballot for the May 12 Annual Town Election. The questions allow voters to decide whether to exclude debt service for major capital projects, including road borrowing, from the constraints of Proposition 2 1/2.
key_details: Ballot question language was drafted and reviewed by Town Counsel Jay Talerman and bond counsel.
The questions correlate directly to capital warrant articles presented at Town Meeting.
Officials noted that the Neary School borrowing was previously approved at Town Meeting regardless of exclusion, while other debt authorizations depend on ballot exclusion.
Board members discussed the cumulative tax impact of recurring debt exclusions outside the tax cap.
topics.outcome: Approved 5-0 to place the debt exclusion questions on the May 12, 2026 town election ballot.
topics.why_it_matters: Approval places major capital borrowing questions on the May ballot, giving voters the final decision on whether to exempt projects from Proposition 2 1/2 tax limits.

votes.motion: Approve the financial policies for investments, ambulance receivables, anti-fraud, reconciliations, and revenue turnover.
Recommend approval of Article 13 as printed in the warrant at Annual Town Meeting.
Approve the debt exclusion ballot questions for the May 12, 2026 Annual Town Election ballot.

public_comment.summary: A resident of Woodland Road urged the town to build a centralized grant-tracking database to monitor grant expiration dates, equipment lifecycles, and future operational budget impacts rather than reacting after grants end.

A resident of Woodland Road suggested removing the income cap on the senior tax work-off program unless slots are oversubscribed, arguing that skilled seniors above the limit could provide valuable professional services to town departments.
